AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
AFG.summary: Non-state provision includes fee-charging private schools, fee-free private religious schools and community- or home-based schools. The profile found no state-funded non-state schools, no contracted schools and no vouchers.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Afghanistan (last modified 21/04/2022)
findings.t: Funding. The profile found no state-funded non-state schools, no contracted schools and no vouchers.

AFG.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

AGO.name: Angola
AGO.mechanism: Law permits state co-financing of private schools
AGO.summary: Angola's education law lets the state co-finance private institutions where there is public or strategic interest. Private schools enrolled 14% of primary pupils in 2015; no use of the co-financing power was documented.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Angola (last modified 25/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Article 57 of the Lei de Bases do Sistema de Educação says the state “may co-finance private institutions” of public or strategic interest. No contracted schools were found.

ALB.mechanism: No public funding found for private schools
ALB.summary: The Eurydice description of Albania's private education names public money only for private higher education scholarships and research, and none for private pre-university schools.

findings.t: Public funding is described only for private higher education (scholarships, research grants).

ALB.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found
ALB.name: Albania

ARE.mechanism: Abu Dhabi charter schools: publicly funded, privately run
ARE.summary: Abu Dhabi's education department launched charter schools in 2018: government schools funded publicly and run by private operators. By 2022 there were 31 schools with 46,500 places.

findings.t: Charter schools 'are publicly funded but privately run'; 22 were open in July 2022 with nine more due that September.

ARE.code_label: Management devolved, money did not move
ARE.name: United Arab Emirates

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary: Argentina funds the teacher, not the child. State subsidies to private schools are calculated and paid against the school's teaching payroll, which makes this the clearest salary-side mechanism in the Americas and a direct test of whether funding the workforce produces a different result from funding the pupil.

findings.t: The mechanism. Subsidies are paid as a proportion of teachers' salary costs. Fee-free schools run by non-profit entities may receive up to 100%; fee-charging schools are banded — category A 80%, B 60%, C 40% of teacher salary costs. To be paid, a school submits its teaching payroll, listing staff, posts, hours and salaries, to the education authority.

Just over 70% of private schools receive state subsidies. About 22% of all students attend subsidized private-management schools, rising to 39% in the City of Buenos Aires, 29% in Córdoba and 26% in Buenos Aires province.
For every 100 pesos the state spends on a public-school student it spends about 55 on a subsidized private-school student (2021).

Why this is the case to watch. Every other system in this Atlas moves money with the pupil and leaves the labour market to sort itself out. Argentina attaches public money directly to teaching posts in non-state schools — the workforce question is inside the funding formula rather than downstream of it.

ARG.mechanism: State subsidy of private-school teacher salaries
ARG.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
ARM.summary: Non-state schools are financed mainly by tuition. Community schools run on government and local budgets, but they are set up by community leaders as non-commercial community organizations, not as private schools.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Armenia (last modified 07/03/2023)
findings.t: Funding. Community schools run on government and local budgets, but they are set up by community leaders as non-commercial community organizations, not as private schools.

ARM.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

ATF.name: French Southern and Antarctic Lands
ATF.shortlist_reason: No permanent population: about 150–310 military, official and research staff are present at a time, and no school system was found to code (Wikipedia, checked Oct 2026).

AUS.mechanism: Commonwealth funds non-government schools at 80% of a standard
AUS.summary: Under the Australian Education Act 2013, the Commonwealth funds non-government schools at a set share of each school's Schooling Resource Standard: at least 80% in 2025. Catholic and independent schools receive about A$19 billion a year.

findings.t: 2025 estimates: A$10.4 billion for Catholic schools and A$8.7 billion for independent schools; payments go to approved bodies.

AUS.name: Australia

AUT.mechanism: The state pays teachers in denominational schools
AUT.summary: Austria grants 100% of teacher personnel costs in denominational private schools; other private schools may be subsidised but are not entitled. About 10% of students attend roughly 600 private institutions, half of them denominational.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. Denominational private schools have 100% of teacher personnel costs paid by the state (Private Schools Act §17); non-denominational schools have no such entitlement (§21).

AUT.code_label: The state pays the teachers, the church runs the schools
AUT.name: Austria

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
AZE.summary: Private schools are funded by private actors under contracts with parents. The only public money found for non-state providers is at pre-school level, where a 2017 law lets municipal and private preschools receive funding to enrol children.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Azerbaijan (last modified 24/03/2023)
findings.t: Funding. The only public money found for non-state providers is at pre-school level, where a 2017 law lets municipal and private preschools receive funding to enrol children.

AZE.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

BDI.name: Burundi
BDI.mechanism: Tax relief and cheap loans, no contracts
BDI.summary: Fewer than 2% of primary pupils but more than half of post-basic pupils attend private schools in Burundi. Private schools are not under contract; the state supports them through customs and tax exemptions and subsidized loans.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Burundi (dernière modification 17/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Private schools “peuvent compter sur l’aide de l’État et bénéficier d’exonérations douanières et fiscales et de prêts à un taux bonifié”. They are not “conventionnées”.

BEL.summary: In Flanders, grant-aided private (mostly Catholic) schools enrol 68% of elementary and secondary pupils. They are subsidised, recognised and inspected by the state on the same footing as official schools.

findings.t: 68% of Flemish elementary and secondary pupils attend grant-aided private schools, subsidised, recognised and inspected by the state.

BEL.code_label: Most pupils in publicly funded private schools
BEL.name: Belgium

BEN.name: Benin
BEN.mechanism: Law allows subsidies; confessional schools under contract
BEN.summary: Benin's law and constitution let private schools receive state subsidies on terms set by decree. Catholic and Methodist schools operate under contract with the state.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Bénin (dernière modification 17/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Under Law 2003-17, Decree 2007-279 and the 1990 Constitution, “les écoles privées peuvent bénéficier des subventions de l’État”.

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.mechanism: State pays private schools to reach 10% of pupils
BFA.summary: Burkina Faso has a policy of supporting private schools so they enrol at least 10% of pupils, funding confessional and community schools through subsidies or per-pupil aid. Private schools must sign a convention with the state.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Burkina Faso (dernière modification 17/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. The state funds confessional and community private schools “par des paiements directs (subventions ou aides par élève)”.

BGD.mechanism: The state pays non-government teachers' salaries (MPO)
BGD.summary: Bangladesh's Monthly Pay Order pays teachers at non-government schools, colleges and madrasas from the state payroll. It began in 1980 at half a government teacher's basic salary and has covered the full basic salary since 2006.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The MPO supports over 27,000 institutions and more than 500,000 educators.

BGD.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child
BGD.name: Bangladesh

BGR.mechanism: Per-pupil state standards, with a free-places condition
BGR.summary: Bulgarian private schools in state financing receive budget funds by a per-pupil standard, on condition that at least 20% of pupils are educated free of charge.

findings.t: Schools must educate 'not less than 20 per cent' of enrolled pupils free of charge; managing bodies hire teachers and appoint directors.

BGR.name: Bulgaria

BHS.name: The Bahamas
BHS.shortlist_reason: The anglophone Caribbean grant-aided pattern is likely to apply, but no Bahamian source establishing it was located in this pass. Shortlisted rather than coded by regional analogy — assuming the pattern is exactly the error this Atlas is meant to avoid.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
BIH.summary: Private schools are a small share of the system (4 of 40 listed high schools in one canton). The profile found no state-funded non-state schools and no contracted schools.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Bosnia and Herzegovina (last modified 02/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. The profile found no state-funded non-state schools and no contracted schools.

BIH.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. No reliable source on public funding of private general schools was found.

BLZ.name: Belize
BLZ.summary: Belize runs one of the most thoroughly pluralistic systems in the hemisphere and almost nobody outside it knows. Denominational and community grant-aided schools are about 62% of all institutions; directly state-managed schools are about 20%. The churches own and manage; the government pays the staff.

findings.t: The mechanism is a payroll, not a voucher. Grant-aided schools are owned by a religious denomination or community group and funded by government through school service grants or direct payment of teachers' salaries.
findings.src: UNESCO Education Profiles — Belize; Notre Dame Education Law Project, country report

findings.t: From 2024 the government committed to 100% of salaries, full pensions and service benefits for 879 teachers and lecturers at grant-aided secondary and tertiary institutions. The 728 teachers at 30 grant-aided secondary schools are 50.7% of all secondary teachers in the country.
findings.src: Breaking Belize News; Love FM Belize

findings.t: Why it matters to the workforce question. Where the state pays the teacher directly, the state holds the workforce lever whoever owns the school. Belize is the clearest case in the Americas of provider pluralism with centralized staffing finance.

BLZ.mechanism: Church–state grant-aided schools; the state pays the teachers
BLZ.code_label: The state pays the teachers, the church runs the schools

BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary: Bolivia funds church-run provision through longstanding convenio agreements and then did something no other country in this Atlas has done so explicitly: it nationalized teacher preparation. Law 070 of 2010 made the State solely responsible for training new teachers.

findings.t: Written agreements between government and the Catholic Church formalize church provision in education, with limited state financial support; in many remote areas Catholic-run schools are the only schooling available.
findings.src: US State Department religious freedom reporting; Agenzia Fides

findings.t: The credentialing move. Law 070 (2010) nationalized teacher training, through which the State assumes sole responsibility for producing new teachers for a secular state. The Catholic teacher-training institute Sedes Sapientiae was closed; the Bolivian Episcopal Conference has pursued the case internationally.

Why this is the sharpest case in the Atlas for WMFC's question. Bolivia kept provider pluralism at the school level and eliminated it at the preparation level. England moved teacher training away from universities and supply fell; Bolivia moved it to the state outright. Both are experiments in who is permitted to make teachers — and both were run without anyone measuring the workforce consequence.

BOL.mechanism: Church–state convenio schools; teacher training nationalized

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary: Brazil's main basic-education funding mechanism, FUNDEB, distributes resources according to enrolment in public schools. Private basic schools receive no subsidy. The country's best-known choice-adjacent programme, PROUNI, operates at higher education and works through tax exemption rather than portability.

findings.t: FUNDEB resources are distributed by the number of students enrolled annually in public schools maintained by each government entity, with a federal top-up to a minimum per-student value. The formula is per-pupil but not portable — it does not follow a child into a private school.
findings.src: OECD, Education in Brazil; Brazilian constitutional framework

findings.t: Brazil does not subsidize private basic-education schools.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: The instructive contrast. PROUNI grants tax exemptions to private higher-education institutions in exchange for scholarships. Brazil has therefore built a large portable-ish mechanism at university level and none at school level — the reverse of the American sequence.

BRA.code_label: Per-pupil funding that is not portable

BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.mechanism: One private school fully funded by the Sultan
BRN.summary: Private schools in Brunei are independent and self-funded. The exception is Al-Falaah, a private school fully funded by the Sultan to model Qur'anic and academic excellence.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Brunei Darussalam (last modified 22/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “Al-Falaah school is a private school fully funded by His Majesty the Sultan.” No contracted non-state schools were found.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary: Private schools in Bhutan are independent. The state funds monastic education institutes, which are owned and governed by the Zhung Dratshang, the constitutionally recognized monastic body, with their own curriculum and exams.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Bhutan (last modified 18/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. The state “funds and supports the establishment of state monastic education institutes”, which are independently regulated by the Zhung Dratshang.

BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.mechanism: A few mission schools receive recurrent state grants
BWA.summary: Most private schools in Botswana are for-profit and unaided. A few Catholic and Congregational mission schools are aided: maintained wholly or partly by recurrent state grants, with fees and curriculum set by the ministry. Aided schools were about 1% of schools in 2017.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Botswana (last modified 22/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Aided schools are “maintained wholly or partially through recurrent state grants or loans” and charge fees set by the ministry.

CAF.name: Central African Republic
CAF.mechanism: All accredited private schools eligible for subsidy
CAF.summary: In the Central African Republic, all private schools that meet state criteria and are accredited are eligible for state subsidies, with additional subsidies for schools taking AIDS orphans. The number funded is unknown.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — République centrafricaine (dernière modification 22/07/2024)
findings.t: Funding. “Tous les établissements privés sont éligibles à des subventions de l’État” if accredited.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary: Canada has no national school-choice policy and never has. Education is a provincial power, and one province went considerably further than the rest. Alberta passed charter legislation in 1994 — still the only Canadian province with charter schools — and funds students in independent schools at 70% of the public per-pupil rate, the highest level in the country. The federal government has no role in any of it.

findings.t: Alberta's charter legislation passed in 1994; the first three schools opened in 1995. Charter schools cannot charge tuition and receive the same per-pupil funding as other public schools. As of 2022–23 roughly 11,000 students were enrolled, about 1.4% of the province's students — three decades of availability at very small scale.
Alberta funds independent-school students at 70% of the public rate, the highest in Canada, and has moved to partially fund independent school construction — a provincial first.

The workforce finding. Alberta's Teaching Quality Standard is the basis of certification for all Alberta teachers and applies across all of the province's publicly funded school authorities, including its charter school divisions. Alberta diversified who may operate a school without changing who may teach in one. Provider pluralism, single credential.

CHE.mechanism: Cantonal choice: little public money for private schools
CHE.summary: Switzerland leaves private schooling to the cantons. Some support private schools or contribute to fees, but 93.7% of compulsory-school pupils attend state schools.

findings.t: Private schools must be approved and supervised; approval requires teaching standards, including teachers, comparable to state schools.

CHE.name: Switzerland

CHL.summary: The longest-running universal voucher, introduced in 1981 on a Chicago-school design. About 91% of enrollment sat under a voucher scheme by 2018, with for-profit operation permitted for nearly 30 years — the most complete arc from deregulation to re-regulation anywhere.

findings.t: The 2015 Ley de Inclusión banned profit-taking in publicly funded schools (two-thirds of voucher schools were for-profit), ended copayments, and replaced school-side selection with a centralized lottery — forcing a restructuring of who may operate.
The widely cited verdict: unregulated choice produced flat scores and widening rich–poor gaps; only added regulation began to deliver gains. Segregation moved on fee rules, not choice itself.

CHL.name: Chile

CHN.mechanism: Private compulsory schooling curbed by design
CHN.summary: China's 2021 revision of its private-education regulations barred public schools from running private branches and closed the door to foreign and acquisition-based control of compulsory-level private schools. Provinces then capped or froze private primary and middle schools.

findings.t: From 1 September 2021, public schools may not take part in organizing private schools; foreign-controlled entities may not run compulsory-level private schools; boards must be Chinese nationals and foreign teaching materials are barred.
In 2021 Hunan and Jiangsu planned to cap private primary and secondary enrolment below 5%; Sichuan stopped approving new private schools and barred expansion.

CHN.name: China

CIV.name: Ivory Coast
CIV.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. World Bank work analyses public subsidies to private schools, but the readable summary did not state the mechanism or scale.

CMR.mechanism: Annual subsidy to secular and religious private schools
CMR.summary: Cameroon pays an annual subsidy to private secular and religious schools; in 2020 it released CFAF 6.5 billion as the balance of its 2019 envelope.

findings.t: The subsidy aims at 'alleviating the costs of running private secular and religious institutions'; what it covers, including teacher pay, is not specified.

CMR.name: Cameroon

COD.mechanism: Church networks run most public schools; parents pay most costs
COD.summary: In the DRC, religious networks, mostly Catholic, manage about 75% of public schools under agreements with the state. Despite a constitutional promise of free education, parents still finance about 80% of schooling costs.

findings.t: Workforce. Churches press the state to 'pay all teachers decently'; free primary education has not been effectively financed.

COD.name: Democratic Republic of the Congo

COG.name: Republic of the Congo
COG.mechanism: Contracted private schools, under 3% of establishments
COG.summary: Congo's contracted private schools (types 1 and 2) can receive state funding; they were 2.82% of establishments in 2015. Private specialized schools also receive continued support.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Congo (dernière modification 10/02/2023)
findings.t: Funding. “Les établissements conventionnés de types 1 et 2 peuvent recevoir un financement de l’État. Ils constituent 2,82 % des établissements en 2015.”

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary: Colombia ran the most rigorously evaluated voucher programme ever built and then stopped running it. PACES was established in late 1991, reached more than 125,000 pupils, allocated places by lottery where demand exceeded supply, and was wound up by the late 1990s. What replaced it — concession schools and subsidies to non-profit private schools — is quieter and still in place.

findings.t: PACES vouchers covered roughly half the cost of private secondary schooling for children in the two lowest socioeconomic strata, and were allocated by lottery when oversubscribed. Lottery winners were about 15 percentage points more likely to attend private school, completed more schooling, and scored about 0.2 standard deviations higher; secondary completion rose 15–20%.
findings.src: J-PAL; Angrist, Bettinger, Bloom, King & Kremer

findings.t: The supply side is where it failed. Low-quality for-profit schools were created to capture voucher revenue, prompting restrictions on which schools could participate. Many established private schools declined to take part — just under half of private schools in the ten largest cities accepted vouchers in 1993. Voucher value was not indexed and eroded with inflation, and payments to schools were delayed. Colombian scholarship describes the programme as una experiencia fallida.
findings.src: Bettinger, Lessons from Private-School Vouchers in Colombia; Colombian programme literature

findings.t: Colombia today subsidizes non-profit private schools, religious and secular, and funds concesionadas — non-profit secular charter-type schools operating with public money.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: The lesson for the workforce question. Demand-side money produced entry by providers who could not sustain quality, and non-entry by providers who could. Nobody in the PACES literature asks where the teachers for the new schools were to come from — which is precisely the seam.

COL.mechanism: PACES vouchers (1991–98), then concession schools and subsidies

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary: Costa Rica made education free and compulsory in 1869, among the earliest anywhere, and built a strong state system around that commitment. Private schools operate and charge fees; public money does not follow students into them.

findings.t: Preschool and basic education are free and compulsory, a constitutional commitment dating to 1869. The system's identity is built on universal state provision rather than provider choice.
findings.src: Education in Costa Rica — country overview

findings.t: Limit. Costa Rica does not appear in the IDB's regional classification of subsidized private-school categories, and no national subsidy mechanism was identified in this pass. Coded as no portability found, not as no portability possible.

CRI.code_label: Universal state provision, no portability found

CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary: Cuba nationalized all schools in 1961 and has maintained the most complete state monopoly in the hemisphere since. There are no faith schools, no charter schools and no semi-private academies. Recent regulation has reaffirmed the prohibition on private education businesses.

findings.t: Schools were nationalized in 1961; regulatory updates have reaffirmed the prohibition on private education enterprises, keeping the state monopoly intact.
findings.src: Right to Education country review — Cuba; Independent Institute

findings.t: The value of the case. Cuba is the region's zero point. Any claim that portable funding is inevitable, or that provider pluralism follows automatically from demand, has to account for a system that has held the opposite line for sixty-five years.

CYP.summary: Cyprus helps pay private-school fees for Turkish Cypriot and minority religious children and subsidises some kindergartens; most private schooling is fee-funded and ministry-supervised.

findings.t: The ministry approves private schools' curricula and fees; fee support is limited to specific groups of children.

CYP.name: Cyprus

CZE.mechanism: Private and church schools funded per pupil
CZE.summary: Czech private schools receive public subsidies under the 1999 Act on subsidies to private schools; denominational schools are funded on the same basis as ministry schools. Private schools enrol 16% of upper secondary pupils but about 3% at basic level.

findings.t: 2024/25 private-school shares: 4.3% of nursery, 3.2% of basic and 16.1% of upper secondary pupils. Schools must be registered to receive state funding and are inspected as public schools are.

CZE.name: Czech Republic

DEU.mechanism: Constitutional right to found private schools, with a right to public funding
DEU.summary: Germany's Basic Law (Art. 7.4) guarantees the right to establish private schools, and approved substitute schools have a right to funding from the Länder, benchmarked on per-pupil spending in state schools, usually after a two- to three-year wait.

findings.t: Approval depends on the workforce. A substitute school is approved only if the economic and legal status of its teachers is secured: written contracts, sufficient pay and pension rights. Teachers need qualifications comparable to the state system; most completed state teacher training.
Private primary schools are allowed only under strict conditions, such as a special pedagogical interest.

DEU.code_label: Funding conditioned on how teachers are treated
DEU.name: Germany

DJI.name: Djibouti
DJI.mechanism: Recognized private schools may receive state aid
DJI.summary: Recognized private schools associated with public education in Djibouti can receive state financial aid; at pre-school level, access to subsidies depends on performance indicators. Madrasas are funded by parents.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Djibouti (dernière modification 24/07/2023)
findings.t: Funding. “Les établissements privés reconnus, associés à l’enseignement public, peuvent recevoir une aide financière de l’État.”

DNK.summary: Danish free private primary and lower secondary schools receive state operating grants calculated mainly on pupil numbers, and parents pay a modest fee on top. Public schools remain the majority.

findings.t: Teaching in private schools must meet what is normally required in the municipal folkeskole; grants follow pupil numbers and reported activity.

DNK.name: Denmark

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary: The Dominican Republic subsidizes private schools — for-profit and non-profit, religious and secular. Private enrolment has been stable at about 26%, one of the larger private shares in the region.

findings.t: Private for-profit and non-profit schools, religious and secular, receive government subsidies; a parallel non-subsidized private sector operates alongside them.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: Private enrolment has been stagnant at about 26% over the decade to 2014 — a large sector that is not growing, in contrast to Chile, Colombia, Argentina, Brazil and Peru.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

DOM.mechanism: Subsidies to private schools, religious and secular

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
DZA.summary: Algeria authorizes private schools, but the profile found no information on public funding for them.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Algérie (dernière modification 16/07/2024)
findings.t: Funding. The section on state-funded non-state schools records that no information was found.

DZA.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary: Ecuador operates a distinct category: fiscomisional schools, religious schools holding an agreement with the government that receives subsidies to pay teacher salaries. Ecuador is also the only country in the region's classification that prohibits for-profit non-subsidized schools.

findings.t: Fiscomisional schools are religious schools with a government agreement, subsidized specifically to pay teacher salaries — a second salary-side mechanism in the region alongside Argentina's.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: Ecuador is the only country in the IDB's regional classification that bans for-profit non-subsidized private schools. The state regulates the ownership form, not only the funding.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: Private enrolment has been stable at about 27% over the decade to 2014.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

ECU.mechanism: Fiscomisional schools — subsidized to pay teacher salaries
ECU.code_label: Subsidy tied to teacher salaries, for-profit barred

EGY.mechanism: A private-share target, without public money
EGY.summary: Egypt's national plan targets a larger private-school share by 2030, from about 12.7% today, through easier licensing rather than public funding of private schools.

findings.t: No direct public funding for private schools is described; the state eases licensing for private nurseries and early-childhood classrooms.

EGY.name: Egypt

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
ERI.summary: Non-government schools are established, managed and financed by non-state actors, and only a few students attend them. No public funding of non-state schools was found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Eritrea (last modified 09/02/2026)
findings.t: Funding. No public funding of non-state schools was found.

ERI.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

ESP.mechanism: Conciertos: publicly funded agreements with private schools
ESP.summary: Spain funds private schools through 'educational agreements' (conciertos) set in the state budget, covering salaries and maintenance. A third of general schools are private, and most of those receive public money.

findings.t: Of 9,385 private general schools in 2023/24, 5,854 received public funds through agreements. General agreements fully fund compulsory education.

Workforce. Agreement amounts include staff salaries, and teacher selection in publicly funded private schools is subject to public oversight. Legal basis: Constitution Art. 27.6 (1978) and the LODE (1985).

ESP.code_label: Agreements cover salaries, private bodies hire
ESP.name: Spain

EST.mechanism: The state pays private-school teachers' labour costs
EST.summary: In Estonia the state budget covers teacher and head labour costs and teaching materials in private general schools. 60 of 474 general schools were private in 2025/26.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. State budget funds private schools' teacher and head labour costs, in-service training and teaching materials. Teachers must make up at least a fifth of a private school's board.

EST.name: Estonia

ETH.mechanism: Private schools fee-funded; teachers without public benefits
ETH.summary: Addis Ababa has 1,631 private schools. Only government teachers receive housing allowances, and a 2019 proposal sought transport and housing allowances for private-school teachers.

findings.t: Workforce. Private-teacher pay ranged from 3,000 to 10,000 birr, fully taxed, without the allowances public teachers receive.

ETH.name: Ethiopia

FIN.summary: Finland funds private schools that hold a government licence on the same basis as public schools, but grants licences only where there is an educational need and no profit motive. About 3% of basic schools are private.

findings.t: Licences require an educational or cultural need, adequate resources and no 'financial gain' motive; unlicensed schools get no public funding. Private schools follow national curricula and qualification requirements.

FIN.name: Finland

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.mechanism: 96% of schools are non-state and state-funded
FJI.summary: 96% of Fiji's schools are government-aided committee schools run by faith-based organizations and communities, financed mainly by per-pupil state grants covering infrastructure, staffing, textbooks and management. Independent private schools are about 3%.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Fiji (last modified 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Government-aided schools are “primarily financed by the state through per-pupil grants covering costs in infrastructure, staffing, textbooks, and management.”

FJI.code_label: Most pupils in publicly funded private schools

FLK.name: Falkland Islands
FLK.shortlist_reason: A British overseas territory with a very small school system. Whether UK funding arrangements apply in any portable form was not established. Shortlisted.

FRA.mechanism: Contract schools: the state pays private-school teachers (loi Debré)
FRA.summary: Since 1959, private schools under contract with the state have their teachers paid by the state, while a private body runs the school. About one pupil in six attends private education, almost all of it under contract.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. Under association contracts, teachers are public-sector employees paid by the state but recruited by the school head; under simple contracts the private authority hires and the state pays.
97.9% of private-school pupils attend schools under contract. Local authorities may not fund private primary schools' running costs, but must contribute to contract collèges and lycées.

FRA.code_label: The state pays the teachers, a private body runs the school
FRA.name: France

GAB.name: Gabon
GAB.mechanism: State subsidizes confessional schools and pays much of their staff
GAB.summary: Gabon subsidizes recognized confessional private schools and pays the salaries of a large share of their staff. In 2015, subsidized private schools enrolled 90% of private secondary pupils, 27% of all secondary pupils, and 77% of private primary pupils.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Gabon (dernière modification 09/12/2022)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The state “prend aussi en charge les salaires d’une bonne franche de leurs personnels”.

GAB.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

GBR.summary: England (coded under GBR) is the case that speaks to WMFC's exact institutional question. From 2010 the government deliberately moved initial teacher training away from universities toward schools — treating university-led training as 'the problem' — via School Direct and a target of at least 50% school-led places.

findings.t: Relocating credentialing off the university campus suppressed supply: School Direct ran at ~45% of places filled in an early year, projected to yield thousands fewer teachers, as university places were capped faster than school routes filled.
The transferable lesson: decentralizing credentialing does not automatically create throughput, and can reduce it unless deliberately resourced.

GBR.name: United Kingdom

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Georgia's per-capita financing is often cited as reaching private schools, but no source read confirmed it.

GHA.mechanism: Government-assisted mission schools: the state pays the staff
GHA.summary: Ghana's mission schools are government-assisted: the state provides staff, salaries and grants, while churches claim ownership. Who governs them is now openly contested.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The state provides staff, salaries, subventions and grants-in-aid, but payments are often delayed, so churches, PTAs and alumni fill gaps. The Attorney General says Wesley Girls' is 'owned by the Methodist Church and not the state'.

GHA.code_label: The state pays, the church owns
GHA.name: Ghana

GIN.name: Guinea
GIN.mechanism: Recognized private schools may receive subsidies
GIN.summary: Approved and recognized private schools in Guinea may receive state subsidies; the types were not documented. Until 2016 the state paid private universities directly for state-scholarship students.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Guinée (dernière modification 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Recognized private schools “peuvent recevoir des subventions”; no other information on the type of subsidy was found.

GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary: The Gambia's grant-aided schools are run by religious, charitable or philanthropic bodies, financed mainly by state grants and often treated as part of the state system. They must be non-profit and accept state rules on admissions and fees.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Gambia (last modified 01/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Grant-aided schools “are primarily financed by the state through grants, and often considered part of the state school system”.

GNB.name: Guinea Bissau
GNB.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
GNB.summary: Independent non-state schools sit mainly in urban areas. The profile found no state-funded or contracted non-state schools and no information on subsidies.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Guinea-Bissau (last modified 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. The profile found no state-funded or contracted non-state schools and no information on subsidies.

GNB.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

GNQ.name: Equatorial Guinea
GNQ.mechanism: Concertado schools funded by convenio, mostly Catholic
GNQ.summary: Equatorial Guinea's 2007 General Education Law creates concertado schools: non-state schools that receive state funding, in staff or money, under a convenio setting obligations on staff and pupils. Most are Catholic.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Guinea Ecuatorial (última modificación 21/07/2022)
findings.t: Funding. “Los centros docentes concertados son centros educativos no estales que reciben financiamiento por parte del Estado”; most are Catholic schools receiving state subsidy.

GRC.summary: Greek private primary and secondary schools receive full private funding, with no state funding described. They sit in the same school types as public schools under Law 682/1977.

findings.t: Private schools 'receive full private funding'. Teachers' qualification and pay rules are not set out separately.

GRC.code_label: Permission to operate, no public money
GRC.name: Greece

GRL.name: Greenland
GRL.shortlist_reason: Greenland runs its own school system under a Danish constitutional framework. Whether Denmark's free-school funding model extends to it was not established. Shortlisted pending a Greenlandic or Danish source.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary: Guatemala funds some non-state provision, but narrowly and on condition. Private schools may be subsidized only where they provide services free, serve low-income populations and pursue quality or pedagogical innovation. Cooperative schools are funded jointly by municipality, parents and ministry.

findings.t: Subsidies to qualifying private schools ran to about USD 13.8 million in 2017 — 0.6% of education spending. Non-profit cooperative schools received a further USD 22 million across 1,108 schools, 0.9% of public education spending. Portability exists and is very small.

Public education spending has stayed between 2.8% and 3.3% of GDP since 2006, below the UNESCO benchmark of 4–6%. The constraint on this system is the size of the total envelope, not the rules on who may receive it.

GTM.mechanism: Targeted subsidy conditioned on free provision

GUF.name: French Guiana
GUF.summary: French Guiana is a French département, so French national education law applies in full. That includes the 1959 Loi Debré contract system, under which private schools contracting with the state teach the national curriculum and have their teachers paid by the state.

findings.t: Under the French contract system, schools sous contrat teach the national programme and their teachers are remunerated by the state — a salary-side mechanism rather than a per-pupil voucher, in continuous operation since 1959.
findings.src: Loi Debré (1959), French national education law

findings.t: Limit, stated plainly. This entry is coded from the metropolitan legal framework that governs the territory, not from a territory-specific reading of provision on the ground in French Guiana. Treat the mechanism as established and the local practice as unverified.

GUF.mechanism: French contract system (Loi Debré) applied in an overseas département

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary: Guyana is the reversal case. In 1976 the government took over the country's church and private schools — close to 696 of them — abolished fees at every level and made free education a constitutional right. The dual system the rest of the anglophone Caribbean retained was dismantled here.

findings.t: Close to 696 schools, most privately financed or owned by church organisations, came under state control in 1976. Universal free education from nursery to university was introduced by constitutional amendment that year and entrenched in the 1980 constitution.
findings.src: Stabroek News; Guyana country education histories

findings.t: The stated reason was a staffing question. Before 1976 the churches held major influence over who taught in their schools, who attended and what was taught. Nationalization was justified as ending a dual system in which employment and attendance turned on religion — a portable-funding arrangement undone specifically on who-may-teach grounds.
findings.src: Stabroek News; Guyana country education histories

GUY.mechanism: Nationalized in 1976; universal free state provision

HND.name: Honduras
HND.shortlist_reason: Private enrolment is roughly 20% and financed mainly by family fees; Honduras does not appear among the subsidizing countries in the IDB regional classification. A Notre Dame Education Law Project country report exists and has not yet been read in full. Shortlisted rather than coded because the funding position is inferred from absence rather than read from a Honduran source.

HRV.summary: Croatian private schools are funded by their founders, who must pay salaries and running costs; state co-financing reaches private kindergartens, not schools.

findings.t: For private schools the founder funds salaries and running costs; the state co-finances private kindergartens, where founders set staff pay.

HRV.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found
HRV.name: Croatia

HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary: Haiti is the inverse of every other case in this Atlas. Non-state schools are not an alternative to the state system; they are substantially the system. Subsidies reach private for-profit and non-profit schools, religious and secular.

findings.t: Haiti subsidizes private for-profit and non-profit schools, both religious and secular, alongside a large unsubsidized private sector.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: Why the direction matters. Elsewhere portable funding is a policy choice layered onto an existing state system. In Haiti non-state provision arose from the absence of state capacity, and subsidy follows that reality rather than creating it. Read as an equilibrium case only with that caveat attached.

HTI.mechanism: Subsidies into an overwhelmingly non-state system
HTI.code_label: Non-state by default, not by design

HUN.mechanism: Public education contracts with church and private schools
HUN.summary: Hungarian church and private schools can take on public education tasks under a contract with the minister; education is then free and admission follows state-school rules.

findings.t: Contracted providers must meet national curriculum requirements, staff qualification rules and facility standards, and are scrutinised by government agencies.

HUN.name: Hungary

IDN.mechanism: Per-student school grants reach private schools and madrasahs
IDN.summary: Indonesia's BOS block grant, running since 2005, pays a per-student amount to all public and private primary and junior secondary schools, including madrasahs.

findings.t: BOS 'supports all public and private primary and junior secondary schools', including madrasahs; 2012 rates were Rp 580,000 per primary and Rp 710,000 per junior secondary student.

IDN.name: Indonesia

IND.mechanism: A 25% free-seat quota in private schools, reimbursed by the state
IND.summary: India's Right to Education Act requires private unaided schools to reserve 25% of entry-class seats for disadvantaged children, admitted free by lottery; the state reimburses the school per child at a state-fixed rate.

findings.t: Schools are reimbursed per child at a state-fixed rate, claimed half-yearly (Manipur notification, 2022).
Karnataka proposed reimbursing schools 'up to Rs 13,000 per child' (2011).

IND.code_label: The seat is portable, by quota
IND.name: India

IRL.mechanism: State-funded staffing for denominational and fee-charging schools
IRL.summary: Most Irish schools are privately owned, mostly by churches, and publicly funded. Schools in the Free Education Scheme receive funding for staffing and running costs and may not charge fees; 56 fee-charging private schools still receive reduced staffing funding.

findings.t: Workforce. The Department funds staffing in Free Education Scheme schools and gives reduced staffing funding to fee-charging private schools, about 25,000 pupils or 6.7% of post-primary enrolment.

IRL.code_label: The state funds the staff, owners run the schools
IRL.name: Ireland

IRN.summary: About 12% of Iranian pupils attend non-state schools. The state 'is unable to help the non-state education sector', and non-profit schools select their own teachers under state rules.

findings.t: 1.8 million of 14 million pupils were in non-state schools in 2018–19; non-profit schools select teachers 'applying the rules defined by the State'.

IRN.name: Iran

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
IRQ.summary: Private and international schools are owned by individuals and enterprises and charge fees. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Iraq (last modified 03/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

IRQ.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

ISL.mechanism: Municipal funds of at least 75% per pupil
ISL.summary: Accredited private compulsory schools in Iceland receive municipal funds for resident pupils covering at least 75% of the average per-pupil operating cost (Act 91/2008).

findings.t: Private compulsory schools follow the same rules as municipal ones and the National Curriculum Guide.

ISL.name: Iceland

ISR.mechanism: Partial funding tied to partial core curriculum
ISR.summary: Israel funds Haredi 'recognized but unofficial' schools at 75% of public-school budgets on condition they teach 75% of core subjects, and 'exempt' institutions at 55% for 55% of core hours.

findings.t: Workforce. Teachers in these schools need not hold academic degrees, and 76% of schools do not give the ministry full staff details.

ISR.name: Israel

ITA.mechanism: Parity schools: recognized, mostly indirect public money
ITA.summary: Italian 'parity' private schools are recognized as part of the national system under Law 62/2000, but public money reaches them mostly indirectly, through family grants and tax breaks, with direct funding at primary and preschool level.

findings.t: Parity schools must employ qualified teachers on individual contracts aligned with national collective agreements. Families receive student grants and tax breaks; regions may add funds.

ITA.name: Italy

JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary: Jamaica inherited the British colonial dual system and kept it. A substantial share of primary and secondary schools are run by religious denominations — Anglican, Catholic and others — and receive government funding while retaining their religious character.

findings.t: Church-run schools frequently receive government funding while keeping their denominational identity. Religious schools receiving public funds must admit students of all faiths and meet ministry standards — funding is conditioned on open admission.
findings.src: US State Department, International Religious Freedom Report — Jamaica

findings.t: A separate independent sector, governed by its own boards and funded by fees, endowment and donations, sits outside the funded system.
findings.src: Education financing in Jamaica — country overview

JAM.mechanism: Government-funded church schools within the public system

JOR.mechanism: Private schools fee-funded; the workforce question is pay
JOR.summary: Jordan's private schools are fee-funded. The documented policy action is on the workforce: private-school teachers, 88% of them women, were paid below the minimum wage until a 2014 collective contract and inspections.

findings.t: Workforce. A 41.6% gender pay gap and pay below the 190 JD minimum wage prompted a 2014 collective contract on summer salaries, leave and minimum pay.

JOR.name: Jordan

JPN.mechanism: Tuition support follows the student to private high schools
JPN.summary: From fiscal 2026 Japan is making high school largely tuition-free, with subsidies of up to ¥457,200 a year per student at full-time private high schools. The money follows the student, public or private.

findings.t: Draft budget: subsidies of 'up to 457,200 yen per student' a year at full-time private high schools from fiscal 2026.

The workforce worry is on the public side. Public high-school educators fear the narrower cost gap will pull students to private schools and speed consolidation of public schools; the ministry plans support to make public schools more attractive.

JPN.name: Japan

KAZ.mechanism: Per-capita state funding for private schools
KAZ.summary: Kazakhstan pays private schools per student through state contracts: 789 schools in 2026, about 78.7 billion tenge. Audits found students moved between schools 5 to 12 times and schools enrolling twice their capacity.

findings.t: Contracts signed with 789 private schools (845 in 2025); 206 previously funded institutions did not meet requirements, and the Prime Minister ordered the funding mechanism reviewed.

KAZ.name: Kazakhstan

KEN.mechanism: Private schools fill gaps, with little public support
KEN.summary: In parts of Nairobi, children attend private schools because no public school exists nearby. Private and alternative schools 'enjoy little or no government support', and regulation reaches about one in eight institutions a year.

findings.t: Workforce. 'Unqualified teachers' are named as a key challenge in informal-settlement private schools.

KEN.code_label: Non-state by default, not by design
KEN.name: Kenya

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.mechanism: Private schools operate without public subsidy
KGZ.summary: Private schools in Kyrgyzstan operate without subsidies from national, regional or local governments. Private pre-schools receive tax exemptions instead.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Kyrgyzstan (last modified 09/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “Private schools in Kyrgyzstan operate without subsidies from national, regional or local governments.”

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
KHM.summary: Private schools are established, funded and managed by individuals, NGOs or associations. Public money reaches community preschools, which can receive monthly per-teacher state subsidies, but no state-funded non-state schools were found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Cambodia (last modified 26/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Public money reaches community preschools, which can receive monthly per-teacher state subsidies, but no state-funded non-state schools were found.

KHM.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Korean private secondary schools are widely described as state-financed under the equalization policy, but no source read stated who pays private-school teachers. Needs a Korean ministry or KEDI source.

CS-KM.name: Kosovo
CS-KM.mechanism: Government pays one Jesuit school, contested
CS-KM.summary: Kosovo's government has funded the Loyola Gymnasium in Prizren since 2005 under a memorandum making the ministry responsible for staff salaries. Auditors and former ministers call the payments unlawful; other private schools receive nothing.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. A 2004 memorandum states “MEST shall be responsible for the salaries of the staff and teachers”; the government paid €658,858 in 2018. The National Audit Office contests the legal basis.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.mechanism: Private schools subsidized, not fully funded
KWT.summary: Kuwait subsidizes private education without fully funding it: government funds, land for school construction and textbooks. The number of subsidized schools is not published.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Kuwait (last modified 07/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “The government does not fully fund private education, although it is subsidised.” No statistics on the number of subsidized schools were found.

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary: Private schools in Lao PDR are self-funded. Buddhist monk schools are recognized as part of the national system and supported by the government through infrastructure, budget and staffing.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Lao PDR (last modified 10/03/2026)
findings.t: Funding. The government “supports these schools through infrastructure, budget, and staffing.”

LBN.mechanism: Per-pupil grants to 'free private' schools, paid late
LBN.summary: About two-thirds of Lebanese pupils attend private schools. 'Free private' schools, 14% of pupils, receive a state grant per pupil, about $100 million a year, but payments have been incomplete since 2012.

findings.t: Free schools enrol 14% and fee-charging private schools 52% of pupils; the state grant per pupil has been paid incompletely since 2012.

LBN.code_label: The grant follows the pupil, when it is paid
LBN.name: Lebanon

LBR.mechanism: Public schools outsourced to private operators
LBR.summary: Since 2016 Liberia has contracted private operators to manage public schools (Partnership Schools for Liberia, now LEAP). The pilot covered 93 schools and eight operators.

findings.t: After three years, test scores rose 0.21 SD in math and 0.16 SD in English, with results varying by operator; dropout rose. Teachers remained government civil servants.

LBR.name: Liberia

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
LBY.summary: Independent schools follow the national curriculum in Arabic. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Libya (last modified 19/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

LBY.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

LKA.summary: In 1960 Sri Lanka nationalised private schools, taking over about 690 Catholic schools without compensation. Teachers became government employees; few institutions chose to stay private and self-funded.

findings.t: Workforce. Teachers in nationalised schools are now government employees; Apostolic Carmel keeps only one of its 20 schools private.

LKA.code_label: Church schools absorbed into the state
LKA.name: Sri Lanka

LSO.mechanism: Churches own most schools; the state pays the teachers
LSO.summary: Churches own and operate 83% of Lesotho's primary schools and 66% of secondary schools. The Ministry of Education pays and certifies all teachers at government-funded schools, including religious ones.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. 'The Ministry of Education pays and certifies all teachers at government-funded schools, including religious schools.'
findings.src: US State Dept., 2022 Religious Freedom Report

LSO.code_label: The state pays the teachers, the church runs the schools
LSO.name: Lesotho

LTU.summary: Lithuania funds non-state schools per pupil (the 'pupil's basket') and per class, the same mechanism as for state schools. Non-state schools are about 10% of general schools.

findings.t: Non-state schools receive state or municipal funds per pupil and per class; they must employ staff with legally required qualifications.

LTU.name: Lithuania

LUX.mechanism: State subsidies to curriculum-following private schools
LUX.summary: Luxembourg subsidises private schools that teach national or their own curricula under a 2003 law; international private schools receive nothing. About 9% of primary and 19% of secondary pupils attend private schools.

findings.t: Private schools following national or their own curricula receive state subsidies; private international schools receive none (law of 13 June 2003).

LUX.name: Luxembourg

LVA.summary: Accredited private general schools in Latvia can receive state funds for teaching staff salaries, and may agree per-pupil funding with local authorities. Private schools are 14% of general schools.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. State funds cover teaching staff salaries in accredited private general schools; per-pupil amounts are set centrally by the Cabinet of Ministers.

LVA.name: Latvia

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Reports describe teachers leaving private schools for the public sector; the source on scale could not be opened.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Moldova uses per-student financing, but no source read said whether it reaches private schools; the private sector 'plays a minimal role'.

MDG.name: Madagascar
MDG.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. The key source on community-paid (FRAM) teachers and private schools could not be opened.

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.summary: Article 3 of the 1917 Constitution makes the State the provider of free compulsory education. Private entities may operate schools, but only with prior and explicit official recognition of studies, and they teach the national syllabus. Money does not follow the child.

findings.t: Mexico does not subsidize private schools. Private enrolment has been stable at about 9% — the lowest share among the larger Latin American systems and flat over the decade to 2014.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: Private schools must obtain prior authorization from the education authorities and teach to the same purposes, criteria and syllabus as public schools, including for teacher-training colleges. The regulated variable is permission to operate, not funding.
findings.src: Political Constitution of the United Mexican States, Art. 3; Notre Dame Education Law Project, country report

MEX.mechanism: Private provision authorized, not publicly funded
MEX.code_label: Permission to operate, no public money

MKD.name: Macedonia
MKD.shortlist_reason: Eurydice's page on private education in North Macedonia could not be opened in October 2026.

MLI.name: Mali
MLI.mechanism: Exceptional subsidies for public-utility private schools
MLI.summary: In Mali, private schools recognized as of public utility can receive exceptional subsidies (half-bursaries and fees), mainly for fields the state does not offer.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Mali (dernière modification 26/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Recognized public-utility private schools “peuvent recevoir des subventions « exceptionnelles » de l’État”, prioritized for fields absent from state schools.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.mechanism: Monastic schools receive subsidies including teacher pay
MMR.summary: Myanmar's monastic schools follow the national curriculum under the religious affairs ministry, and the state subsidized them, including teachers' salaries, under the 2016–21 strategic plan. In 2017/18 there were 909 monastic primary, 646 middle and 2 high schools.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Myanmar (last modified 09/06/2023)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. “The state provides subsidies to these types of schools including teachers’ salaries payments.” Status after the 2021 coup was not checked.

MMR.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

MNE.mechanism: No public funding found for private schools
MNE.summary: Montenegro funds private institutions only for higher-education programmes of public interest that no public institution offers.

findings.t: State funds reach private higher education only for 'study programmes of public interest'.

MNE.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found
MNE.name: Montenegro

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.mechanism: Private schools entitled to per-student state funding
MNG.summary: Mongolia's Law on Education entitles private schools to state per-student funding on top of their own financing; a 2016 government decree sets the amount.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Mongolia (last modified 07/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “Private schools are entitled to state financing through per student funding mechanism based on the amount of tuition fee.”

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.mechanism: Some community schools receive state-posted teachers
MOZ.summary: Private schools are Mozambique's main form of non-state provision and are fee-funded. Some community schools receive government support, mainly teacher postings, and charge no fees.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Mozambique (last modified 03/12/2021)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. “Some community schools receive support from the government, mainly in the form of teacher postings.”

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.mechanism: Funded community schools at public per-pupil rates
MRT.summary: State-funded private schools in Mauritania are mostly community schools, many with a cultural or religious mission. The government sets their curriculum, and their academic operating budgets equal per-pupil amounts in public schools.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Mauritanie (dernière modification 17/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “Les budgets de fonctionnement académique sont équivalents aux montants par élève dans les écoles publiques.”

MWI.mechanism: Grant-aided church schools staffed with public funds
MWI.summary: Religious bodies in Malawi typically run 'grant-aided' schools: privately run but staffed with public funds. In return the government selects a large share of pupils.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. At grant-aided schools 'their teaching staffs are paid by the government'.
findings.src: US State Dept., 2022 Religious Freedom Report

MWI.code_label: The state pays the teachers, the church runs the schools
MWI.name: Malawi

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Mission schools claim a legal right to grants-in-aid under the Education Act 1996; who pays their teachers was not stated in sources read.

NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary: Namibia's aided private schools are non-profit schools that receive state subsidies, staff or materials. For-profit private schools are unaided.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Namibia (last modified 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “Aided private schools are non-profit private schools in Namibia which are granted different forms of aid by the state (in the form of subsidies, provision of staff and/or material).”

NCL.name: New Caledonia
NCL.mechanism: The French state pays private-school teachers
NCL.summary: In New Caledonia, 24.3% of pupils attend private schools, mostly religious networks under contract. The French state pays their teachers (about 13 billion XPF in 2022); New Caledonia, provinces and communes pay running costs. A 2023 resolution set a legal basis for the rest.

findings.src: Gouvernement de la Nouvelle-Calédonie, press release on private-school funding, 13 Sep 2023
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. Teacher salaries are paid by the State; contracted secondary schools receive about 2.1 billion XPF and primary schools about 300 million XPF a year in running costs.

NCL.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

NER.name: Niger
NER.summary: Niger's state may give private schools, though not Qur'anic schools, subsidies, teacher salaries, seconded teachers and materials. How many schools receive support is not known.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Niger (dernière modification 09/12/2022)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The state may grant “des subventions financières, une prise en charge des salaires des enseignants, une mise à disposition de personnel enseignant”.

NGA.mechanism: Most Lagos children in private schools, by default
NGA.summary: In Lagos State, research found about 70% of children aged 5 to 14 in private schools, most of them low-fee. They emerged without public funding.

findings.t: A 2010 census counted 12,098 private schools in Lagos with 1.4 million pupils; estimates now exceed 16,000 schools.

NGA.code_label: Non-state by default, not by design
NGA.name: Nigeria

NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.shortlist_reason: No national subsidy mechanism was identified and Nicaragua does not appear in the IDB regional classification. No Notre Dame country report is published. Shortlisted because a null this thin should not be published as a coded finding.

NLD.summary: After the century-long Schoolstrijd, the 1917 constitutional settlement funded privately governed schools on equal terms with state schools, subject to central inspection. Roughly 70% of Dutch schools are now run by private boards, all funded equally.

findings.t: A century of the most pluralistic provider system in the world did not immunize the teaching workforce: the Netherlands entered a structural teacher shortage (lerarentekort) flagged since 2011, driven partly by workload and teachers' reported lack of autonomy.
Freedom to establish is inseparable from an obligation to be inspected — portability here is anchored by a strong central Inspectorate, not a free market.

NLD.name: Netherlands

NOR.mechanism: Grants of about 85% for approved alternatives only
NOR.summary: Norway's approved independent schools receive about 85% of their costs as public grants, but approval is limited to religious or recognised pedagogical alternatives, international curricula, special needs and elite sport.

findings.t: Approval grounds are restricted to a religious alternative, a recognised pedagogical alternative or an internationally certified curriculum, among a few others. Most pupils attend municipal schools.

NOR.name: Norway

NPL.mechanism: Private schools grow with no public money; the fight is over teacher pay
NPL.summary: Nepal's private 'institutional' schools receive no government funding, yet enrolment in them rose 47.55% in five years while public enrolment fell 20.14%. Kathmandu now requires private schools to pay teachers on par with community schools.

findings.t: Workforce. Kathmandu's mayor said private schools must pay teachers the same as community-school teachers or face closure (2023).

NPL.name: Nepal

NZL.mechanism: State integration: the state funds teaching, owners keep character
NZL.summary: Since the Private Schools Conditional Integration Act 1975, about 330 mostly Catholic schools have been 'integrated' into the state system: the government funds teaching and operating costs, while proprietors own the land and buildings and charge attendance dues.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The government funds boards for 'the teaching and operating costs'; proprietors keep the property and their special character.

NZL.code_label: The state pays the teachers, the church keeps the character
NZL.name: New Zealand

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
OMN.summary: About 30% of students attended private schools in 2019, yet no public funding of private schooling was found at basic level. Royal Decree 67 of 2000 subsidizes private higher education only.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Oman (last modified 07/01/2022)
findings.t: Funding. Royal Decree 67 of 2000 subsidizes private higher education only.

OMN.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

PAK.summary: Punjab's Education Foundation has run an Education Voucher Scheme since 2006, letting children from low-income areas attend partner private schools free; families choose the school. Education is a provincial matter, so this is not national.

findings.t: About 0.5 million children use vouchers in more than 1,780 partner schools across 36 districts.

PAK.name: Pakistan

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary: Panama has a substantial private sector of about 17% of enrolment, stable over the last decade, funded by fees. The state does not subsidize it.

findings.t: Panama's private schools — for-profit and non-profit, religious and secular — receive no government subsidies. Private enrolment has been flat at roughly 17%.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

PAN.code_label: Large private sector, no public money

PER.name: Peru
PER.summary: Peru is the deregulation case. A 1998 legal decree promoted private investment in education by loosening constraints on opening schools, permitting for-profit operation and offering tax credits to investors. Supply responded sharply. Public subsidy did not follow.

findings.t: The 1998 decree reduced legislative constraints on opening private schools, allowed for-profit operation and offered generous tax credits to investors. Private enrolment rose from 13% in 1998 to 26% in 2014; in Lima non-state participation went from 29% in 2004 to 50% in 2014.
findings.src: Balarin, NORRAG; Right to Education Initiative

findings.t: Public money barely follows. Peru subsidizes only the Fe y Alegría chain of Catholic schools, under 2% of total enrolment.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: The supply-quality result. In mathematics the share of low-achieving students in the low-fee private sector is about three times the public-sector share, and at secondary level the low-fee private sector is the single private modality performing worse than public schools. Regulatory capacity did not scale with the sector: licences are granted by local authorities that perform no regular supervision.
findings.src: OECD, Education and Skills in Peru; Education International

findings.t: Read against Chile. Peru deregulated supply without making money portable; Chile made money portable and then re-regulated supply. Both ended up legislating about who may operate.

PHL.mechanism: Vouchers and contracts with private schools at scale
PHL.summary: The Philippines subsidises private schooling through Education Service Contracting at junior high and the Senior High School Voucher Program. Together they target over 2.4 million learners in 2026–27.

findings.t: About 990,000 junior high students through ESC and 1.47 million senior high students through the voucher program, school year 2026–27.

PHL.name: Philippines

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary: About 46% of schools in Papua New Guinea are church agency schools, owned and run by churches and funded by the state under a government–church partnership that unified the two systems in the 1970s.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Papua New Guinea (last modified 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. Church agency schools “receive funding from the state based on a long standing Government-Church Partnership established in the 1970s.”

POL.mechanism: Per-pupil grant at least equal to public schools
POL.summary: Non-public schools in Poland receive at least the per-pupil amount local governments get for public schools, and much more for pupils with disabilities. About 7.5% of primary pupils attend non-public schools.

findings.t: Non-public schools must employ teachers with qualifications set by the education minister. Funding: 2017 Act on Financing School Education Tasks.

POL.name: Poland

PRI.name: Puerto Rico
PRI.summary: Puerto Rico is the Atlas's clearest example of a court deciding the question twice. Vouchers were ruled unconstitutional in 1994. Act 85 of 2018 created charter-style 'alianza' schools and private-school vouchers, and in 2019 the island's Supreme Court upheld them.

findings.t: Act 85 authorized a public charter system capped at 10% of all public schools and private-school vouchers capped at 3% of students from 2019–20. Both caps are unusually explicit; most systems in this Atlas cap nothing.

A 1994 ruling had held vouchers unconstitutional. In Asociación de Maestros v. Departamento de Educación (2019) the Supreme Court of Puerto Rico held that they were constitutional, overturning a lower court that had relied on the 1994 decision.

Operator restriction is the workforce-relevant clause. A ruling limited operation of alianza schools to the University of Puerto Rico and the island's municipalities — a rare case of a system naming a university as an eligible school operator in statute.
findings.src: CBS News; National Center for the Study of Privatization in Education

PRI.mechanism: Act 85 of 2018 — charter schools and capped vouchers
PRI.code_label: Decided by courts, twice, opposite ways

PRK.summary: Education in North Korea is universal and state-funded; the only privately funded institution identified is a university.

findings.t: Schooling is 'universal and state-funded'; Pyongyang University of Science and Technology is 'the country's only privately funded university'.

PRK.name: North Korea

PRT.summary: Portugal funds private schools through several state contracts: family support, association contracts in underserved areas, sponsorship and cooperation for severe disabilities. The legal basis dates to Law 9/79.

findings.t: Private schools manage their own staff under pedagogical autonomy; the ministry encourages teacher qualification and continuing education.

PRT.name: Portugal

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary: Paraguay provides state funding to schools run by religious groups. The mechanism is documented in reporting on religious freedom rather than in education-finance literature, which is itself a finding about how visible these arrangements are.

findings.t: The government provides state funding for schools run by religious groups.
findings.src: US State Department, International Religious Freedom Report — Paraguay

findings.t: Limit. Scale, start year and funding formula were not established in this pass, and Paraguay's Notre Dame country report is listed but not yet published. The existence of the mechanism is documented; its size is not.

QAT.mechanism: Education vouchers for Qatari children at private schools
QAT.summary: Qatar's ministry pays an education voucher of QR 28,000 a year for Qatari students at approved private schools; in 2026 it offered 3,793 fully covered places at 17 schools and dropped the income limit.

findings.t: Parents pay no tuition beyond the voucher; schools absorb fees above QR 28,000. The former income cap was removed in 2026.

QAT.name: Qatar

ROU.mechanism: Per-pupil basic funding for accredited private schools
ROU.summary: Romania gives accredited private and confessional schools 'basic funding per student', with fees covering the rest.

findings.t: Private-school staff are employed under each school's own rules; pay is negotiated with the founding body's board.

ROU.name: Romania

RUS.mechanism: Regional per-pupil subsidies reach private schools
RUS.summary: Russia's 2012 education law requires regions to subsidise private organisations providing basic general education, using the same regional per-pupil standards as public schools, which include teacher pay.

findings.t: Article 99 of Federal Law 273-FZ: subsidies to private general-education organisations come from regional budgets at regional per-pupil standards; program financing includes teacher pay tied to average salary levels.

RUS.name: Russia

RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. The government 'subsidizes some schools affiliated with religious groups', but scale and teacher pay are not stated.

ESH.name: Western Sahara
ESH.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Schools in the Moroccan-administered territory run under Morocco's regional academy (AREF Laâyoune–Sakia El Hamra), and Morocco itself is shortlisted; schools in the Sahrawi refugee camps are run by the Polisario Front with foreign aid. Coding waits on Morocco.

SAU.mechanism: Support tied to Saudi teachers' pay
SAU.summary: Saudi Arabia's School Support Agreement, run with the Human Resource Development Fund, gives private schools state money tied to the salaries of Saudi teachers, about SR70 million a year across some 3,000 schools (2013).

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The ministry required private schools to submit teachers' monthly salary data or lose the support; schools must answer for delayed teacher pay.

SAU.code_label: Support tied to national teachers' pay
SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
