SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
SDN.summary: Non-state fee-charging schools include international, NGO-managed and other private schools. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Sudan (last modified 22/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

SDN.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

SSD.name: South Sudan
SSD.mechanism: Capitation grants to all non-profit schools
SSD.summary: Most non-state schools in South Sudan are community and faith-based schools run on a non-profit basis. All of them receive state capitation grants and cash transfers for running costs. For-profit private schools are under 5%.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — South Sudan (last modified 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “All non-profit schools in South Sudan are funded by the state through capitation grants and cash transfers to cover operational costs.”

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Catholic private schools are prominent and debated, but no source read stated a state subsidy or teacher-pay arrangement.

SLB.name: Solomon Islands
SLB.mechanism: Per-capita grants to every non-state school
SLB.summary: Under the Solomon Islands' Fee-Free Basic Education Policy, all non-state schools, run by church, community, private and independent education authorities, receive annual per-capita grants, with extra for remote schools.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Solomon Islands (last modified 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “All non-state schools receive annual per capita grants as part of the government’s commitment to operationalize the Fee-Free Basic Education Policy.”

SLE.mechanism: Most schools are government-assisted mission and community schools
SLE.summary: Only 13.8% of Sierra Leone's schools are government-owned. Government-assisted non-state schools, mostly mission schools, provide 70% of education; another 16.2% are fully private.

findings.t: Workforce. Government support can cover teacher salaries in assisted schools, which must fund at least 20% of running costs; community teachers are paid through fees and informal contributions.

SLE.name: Sierra Leone

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary: El Salvador has a stable private sector of about 17% of enrolment which the state does not fund. The country is better known in this literature for EDUCO, which decentralized management of state schools to community associations without making the money portable.

findings.t: Private enrolment has been stagnant at about 17% over the decade to 2014, and El Salvador does not appear among the countries subsidizing private schools in the IDB's regional classification.
findings.src: IDB — Elacqua, Iribarren & Santos, Private Schooling in Latin America

findings.t: The distinction worth carrying. Community management of public schools is not portable funding. EDUCO moved control of hiring and oversight to parent associations while the schools remained public — a governance reform, not a choice reform.
findings.src: WMFC coding, Aug 2026; Notre Dame Education Law Project, country report

SLV.mechanism: Unsubsidized private sector alongside state provision
SLV.code_label: Management devolved, money did not move

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.mechanism: Government cannot subsidize private or community schools
SOM.summary: The federal government is unable to subsidize private or community schools, and Puntland's Education Act defines private schools as schools that receive no grants. Qur'anic schools are funded mainly by communities and private foundations.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Somalia (last modified 29/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “The Federal Government is currently unable to subsidize private or community schools to reduce the burden of school fees on poor families.” Government funding goes to schools managed at least partly by the state.

SRB.mechanism: No public funding found for private schools
SRB.summary: Serbia's private schools must show funds for a year of operation and meet staffing and facility requirements; the Eurydice description names no public funding.

findings.t: Founders must show funds for a year's operation and provide prescribed teachers, equipment and facilities.

SRB.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found
SRB.name: Republic of Serbia

SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.shortlist_reason: Suriname inherited the Dutch bijzonder onderwijs model, which would make it one of the more interesting cases in the hemisphere given the Netherlands entry. No Surinamese source was located in this pass. Shortlisted and flagged as a priority.

SVK.mechanism: Equal per-pupil funding for private and church schools
SVK.summary: Slovak private and church schools receive the same per-pupil normative funding as state schools, covering salaries, operations, assistants, textbooks and transport. About 9% of basic-school pupils attend them.

findings.t: Private and church schools are co-financed by the state at the same per-pupil normative as state schools (Act on financing schools, 597/2003).

SVK.name: Slovakia

SVN.mechanism: 85% of public funding for private schools
SVN.summary: Slovenian private schools receive 85% of the funding for the equivalent public programme, or 100% if accredited before 1996. Only about 1% of basic-school pupils attend them.

findings.t: Funding rule set by the 1996 Organisation and Financing of Education Act; private higher vocational colleges must meet public-equivalent staffing requirements.

SVN.name: Slovenia

SWE.summary: A 1992 reform let independent 'free schools' — including for-profit chains, some stock-market-listed — open with light requirements, charge no tuition, follow the national curriculum, and draw equal per-student funding. Free schools now enroll roughly 18% of students.

findings.t: The incentive structure reached teachers' own professional judgment: researchers and center-right politicians debate a documented grade-inflation pattern as a competitive response to enrollment-based funding.

By 2025 the government's own inquiry proposed barring new operators from extracting profit for five years and giving municipal schools more per-student funding for their duty to staff places for every child.

SWE.name: Sweden

SWZ.name: Swaziland
SWZ.mechanism: Government employs and pays mission-school teachers
SWZ.summary: Mission schools are the main non-state provider in Eswatini (29%). They are owned by religious organizations, run on a non-profit basis, and the government employs and pays their teachers.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Eswatini (last modified 07/12/2021)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. Faith-based government-aided schools are run by religious organizations, “with the government employing and paying their teachers.”

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.mechanism: Sharia schools part-funded by the state and the Zakat fund
SYR.summary: About 220 Sharia schools received some government funding in 2013, with much of their money from the government-managed Zakat fund. Private institutions otherwise receive no financial aid.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Syrian Arab Republic (last modified 22/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “While Sharia schools receive some funding from the government, much of their funding comes from the government-managed Zakat fund.”

TCD.name: Chad
TCD.mechanism: Contracted private schools receive staff and textbooks
TCD.summary: Chad's contracted private schools must be accredited and sign an administrative, financial and pedagogical convention with the ministry. They receive subsidies in the form of staff allocations and textbooks.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Tchad (dernière modification 09/12/2022)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. “Les écoles privées conventionnées bénéficient des subventions sous forme d’allocation en personnel et de dotation en manuels scolaires.”

TCD.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

TGO.name: Togo
TGO.mechanism: The state pays the director of community schools
TGO.summary: Togo's local-initiative schools (JEDIL, EDIL, CEGIL, LYDIL) are community-built, mostly rural, and supported by NGOs. The state pays each school's director and bans fees. Policy aims to absorb them into the public system.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Togo (dernière modification 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “Le directeur est rémunéré sur le budget de l'État et le droit de perception des frais de l'école est interdit.” JEDIL enrolled 6.5% of pupils in 2020.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Togo (dernière modification 30/11/2021)
findings.t: Reversal planned. The 2020–30 sector plan aims to phase out the EDIL by 2025 by integrating them into public schools.

THA.name: Thailand
THA.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Sources conflict: a private-school association says government 'has never helped a private school', while ministry budgets mention per-student subsidies. Needs the Office of the Private Education Commission's own figures.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
TJK.summary: Religious bodies may open independent schools. The state funds about 30 NGO-run daycare centres set up to keep children out of residential institutions, but no public funding of non-state schools was found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Tajikistan (last modified 26/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. The state funds about 30 NGO-run daycare centres set up to keep children out of residential institutions, but no public funding of non-state schools was found.

TJK.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary: The profile found no information on any non-state education institutions operating in Turkmenistan.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Turkmenistan (last modified 05/04/2023)
findings.t: Provision. “No information was found on the existence of non-state education institutions in Turkmenistan.”

TKM.code_label: Universal state provision, no portability found

TLS.name: East Timor
TLS.mechanism: School grants extend to private schools
TLS.summary: Timor-Leste's 2008 Education Law commits the state to support private and cooperative education pedagogically, technically and financially, and the school grants policy since 2004/05 covers private schools. Private schools enrolled 14.2% of primary and 32.6% of secondary pupils in 2019.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Timor-Leste (last modified 26/11/2021)
findings.t: Funding. “The school grants policy was introduced in 2004/05 and applies to public and private schools at primary, secondary, and technical/professional levels.”

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary: Signed on 22 December 1960, the Concordat between the State and the denominational boards is one of the longest continuously running portable-funding arrangements in the Americas — sixty-six years. The state pays; the denominations own, manage and, within limits, select.

findings.t: Under the Concordat the state pays salaries and a share of upkeep at denominational schools, which became known as 'government assisted' schools. Ownership and the right of direct control and management remained with the denominations. The arrangement is known locally as the dual system.
findings.src: Concordat Watch; Trinidad and Tobago Newsday

findings.t: The staffing clause is the point. Teachers are selected by both government and denominational boards, and a denominational authority may request the removal of a teacher found unsatisfactory on moral or religious grounds. Denominational schools may also fill 20% of first-form places at their own discretion, the state filling the other 80% by examination.
findings.src: Concordat Watch — text of the 1960 Concordat

findings.t: What sixty-six years has produced. The arrangement remains politically live: national debate continues over equity in the school system and whether the 20% discretionary intake should survive. Duration has not settled the question.
findings.src: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday; Global Voices

TTO.mechanism: The Concordat of 1960 — state-funded denominational schools

TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.mechanism: Subsidies up to 25% of Tunisian teachers' salaries
TUN.summary: Private schools in Tunisia that follow the public curriculum can receive land, investment premiums, tax exemptions and subsidies of up to 25% of the salaries owed to their Tunisian teachers. About 7% of primary pupils were in private schools in 2018.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Tunisie (dernière modification 09/12/2022)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The state offers “des subventions (dans la limite de 25 % des salaires dus aux enseignants tunisiens)”.

TUN.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

TUR.mechanism: Fee-funded private schools, SEN support only
TUR.summary: Turkish private schools are generally funded by tuition; public money reaches them only through support payments for special educational needs. Private schools must educate at least 3% of students free.

findings.t: Private institutions are funded through fees; support education payments under the Law on Private Education Institutions cover special-needs centres.

TUR.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found
TUR.name: Turkey

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Tuition subsidies for private high schools are reported in news coverage, but no source read stated the mechanism and amounts precisely enough to code.

TZA.name: United Republic of Tanzania
TZA.shortlist_reason: Searched October 2026. Research documents low-cost private secondary schools with spare capacity; public funding arrangements were not stated in sources read.

UGA.mechanism: Per-student payments to low-cost private secondary schools
UGA.summary: When Uganda introduced Universal Secondary Education in 2007, it also paid participating low-cost private schools a fixed amount per student to take USE students: 47,000 shillings a term in 2011.

findings.t: An evaluation of 101 schools found higher enrolment and test-score gains, and 'a higher proportion of teachers in PPP schools were present during unannounced school visits'.

UGA.name: Uganda

UKR.mechanism: Per-pupil subvention can pay private-school teachers
UKR.summary: Private Ukrainian schools providing full general secondary education may receive the state educational subvention, transferred to local budgets and used to pay teachers' salaries, by a per-pupil formula.

findings.t: The money follows the teacher. The subvention is used for teachers' salaries; private general secondary schools were 3.6% of institutions in 2023/24.

UKR.name: Ukraine

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary: Uruguay built early and thoroughly on free public provision. Education is free at primary, secondary and most higher levels, financed mainly from public funds, with a small private sector alongside it.

findings.t: The system is mainly financed by public funds, with household contributions, a small private sector and some international aid. No national portable-funding mechanism was identified.
findings.src: Education financing in Uruguay — country overview

findings.t: Limit. Uruguay's Notre Dame Education Law Project country report is listed but not yet published, and no Uruguay-specific subsidy category appears in the IDB regional classification. Coded as none found rather than none possible.

URY.mechanism: Predominantly public financing; small private sector

USA.name: United States of America
USA.summary: The young case. Milwaukee's 1990 voucher programme was the first modern instance; thirty states now fund students rather than systems and eighteen do so universally. The United States has moved faster than any country in this Atlas and has had the least time to discover what the mature systems already show.

findings.t: Roughly 750,000 American children learn in microschools, and more than 70% of the people running them are current or former licensed teachers — the sector is staffed by the preparation system's own graduates.
87% of teachers report feeling prepared to teach in a district school; 34% for a microschool. The 53-point gap has not moved since 2023.
findings.src: EdChoice survey data, via the WMFC Readiness Index

findings.t: The institutional response. Across 39 coded institutions in 9 states, exactly one preparation programme built for the sector was found — Central Michigan's Charter School Leadership M.A. Where universities have entered, they have done it by authorizing or operating schools, not by building degrees. Completing Michigan's eight university authorizers produced no further programmes.

USA.mechanism: State vouchers, tax-credit scholarships and education savings accounts

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
UZB.summary: Private schools are established, operated and financed by non-state actors. Public support for private providers was found only at pre-school level, through public-private partnerships.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Uzbekistan (last modified 03/03/2023)
findings.t: Funding. Public support for private providers was found only at pre-school level, through public-private partnerships.

UZB.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary: Venezuela's private schools operate under a state that has repeatedly asserted the power to close or take over schools that decline its curriculum and inspection regime. The governing question here is control of content and continued permission to operate, not funding.

findings.t: All schools, public and private, must admit state inspectors and adopt the government's educational system or face closure and nationalization, a position asserted publicly by the government during the curriculum reforms of the late 2000s.

Limit. Venezuela does not appear in the IDB's regional classification of subsidized private-school categories, and no current national subsidy mechanism was identified. Current administrative practice was not verified from primary Venezuelan sources in this pass.

VEN.mechanism: Private schools under state curricular control
VEN.code_label: Permission to operate is the live variable

VNM.mechanism: 'Socialisation': incentives to invest, not money per pupil
VNM.summary: Vietnam's 2019 Resolution 35 set targets for non-public schools, 13.5% of institutions by 2025, supported by tax incentives and investment rules rather than per-pupil public funding.

findings.t: Workforce. Non-public K–12 teachers must hold pedagogy degrees, the same as public teachers; incentives are a 10% corporate income tax rate and VAT relief.

VNM.name: Vietnam

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.mechanism: Church schools funded for salaries and running costs
VUT.summary: Most non-state schools in Vanuatu are government-assisted church schools: 31% of primary and 39% of secondary schools. Regular state grants cover teacher salaries and operating costs under funding agreements.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Vanuatu (last modified 01/12/2021)
findings.t: The money follows the teacher. These schools “receive regular grants from the state which cover teacher salaries and operational costs based on a funding agreement with the government.”

VUT.code_label: The money follows the teacher, not the child

PSE.name: West Bank
PSE.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
PSE.summary: Private schools, including international schools, were 14.3% of schools in 2020. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Palestine (last modified 10/03/2026)
findings.t: Funding. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

PSE.code_label: Private schools allowed, no public funding found

YEM.mechanism: Private schools permitted; no public funding found
YEM.summary: Private schools are 2–5% of schools; in 2007/08, 3% of primary and secondary schools were non-state. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

findings.src: UNESCO GEM Report, PEER profile: Non-state actors in education — Yemen (last modified 02/12/2021)
findings.t: Funding. No state-funded or contracted non-state schools were found.

ZAF.summary: South Africa's Schools Act allows provinces to subsidise independent schools, with lower-fee schools eligible for more. In Gauteng, 279 of 1,083 independent schools are subsidised, about R1.13 billion in 2026/27.

findings.t: Gauteng's independent sector serves 379,727 pupils; only 279 schools qualify for subsidies, which scale down as fees rise.

ZMB.mechanism: Grant-aided church schools strained by free education
ZMB.summary: Zambia's grant-aided church schools operate in partnership with government. After free education was introduced in 2022, rising enrolment forced them to hire contract teachers whose pay had come from fees and parent associations.

findings.t: Workforce. Catholic bishops: 'Subsidies from the government are not enough and are usually restrictive'; contract-teacher pay lost its funding source.
